one_liner: Rust reimplementation of MeCab's Viterbi lattice tokenizer for Japanese; about 2x faster than MeCab on IPADIC and UniDic.
what_it_does: Japanese morphological analysis (word segmentation plus POS features) with MeCab's min-cost lattice algorithm and MeCab-format dictionaries (IPADIC, UniDic, JUMAN, NAIST-jdic) converted into its own zstd-compressed binary format. The API is Rust only: build a Tokenizer from a Dictionary, create a Worker per thread, call reset_sentence() and tokenize(), then read tokens (surface, byte/char range, feature string). A tokenize CLI prints MeCab-style or -O wakati output, and a Python wrapper (python-vibrato) exists; it also trains CRF costs from a corpus.
how_it_is_fast: Same Viterbi min-cost search as MeCab, with a lexicon in a crawdad double-array trie and a lattice indexed by end position whose best predecessor is computed when each node is inserted. The main gain is cache locality of the connection-cost matrix: left/right connection ids are renumbered by occurrence frequency gathered from a training corpus (the map/reorder tool), so hot matrix cells sit together; the NLP2023 paper (C2-4, snippet only, the PDF host was unreachable) reports about 40% from this and over 2x vs MeCab. Compact models trade speed for size: raw-connector (mecab_smalldic-style) and dual-connector score splitting.
when_to_use: Batch or server-side Japanese tokenization in Rust where per-sentence latency matters and the dictionary is loaded once per process.
Large-matrix dictionaries such as unidic-cwj 3.1.1 (459 MiB matrix), where the measured gap to MeCab was largest (75 vs 179 ms on the benchmark corpus).
IPADIC-based pipelines that can use the precompiled, id-remapped release dictionaries (42 vs 87 ms for MeCab on the same corpus).
Projects that want to train or re-cost a MeCab-style dictionary on their own corpus without the C++ toolchain.
when_not_to_use: Short-lived processes or CLIs that tokenize a little text: the dictionary is fully deserialized into RAM, and a user reported about 14 s and about 1 GB to load UniDic cwj 2023-02 vs 28 ms for MeCab's mmap (issue #150, open; no mmap support, #148).
Memory-constrained or embedded targets: the maintainers point such users to Vaporetto, since the full unidic-cwj 3.1.1 model is listed at 717 MB.
When output must match MeCab byte for byte: defaults differ (spaces become tokens, unknown-word grouping is unbounded), and even with -S -M 24 the README admits tie-break corner cases.
C or C++ codebases that would need an FFI layer; there is no C API in the repo.
The raw-connector compact UniDic model if speed matters: it measured 1364 ms, 7.6x slower than MeCab.

integration.dependencies: bincode 2, crawdad, csv-core, hashbrown, regex; rucrf for the default-on train feature; the caller needs zstd or ruzstd to decompress the distributed system.dic.zst
integration.min_toolchain: Rust 1.88 at HEAD (rust-version in vibrato/Cargo.toml); crates.io 0.5.2 declares 1.85
integration.platforms: any 32- or 64-bit Rust target (compile_error otherwise); a Wasm demo exists; no CPU feature required, though the benchmark build added +avx2
integration.thread_safety: not documented; the API shape is one immutable Tokenizer shared by reference and one Worker per thread, since a Worker owns the mutable lattice and sentence buffers
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — same algorithm and source dictionaries, but a Rust API, its own binary dictionary format (converted from MeCab resources), and MeCab-identical output only with ignore_space and max_grouping_len 24, minus tie-break corner cases

gotchas: The headline speed depends on remapped connection ids: the v0.5.0 release models were reordered with statistics from BCCWJ v1.1 CORE (v0.4.0 used Aozora Bunko text). A dictionary you compile yourself is slower until you run the map/reorder step from docs/map.md on representative text.

Dictionary::read() expects decompressed bytes; the distributed models are zstd files that must be wrapped in a decoder first. The format is tied to the 'VibratoTokenizer 0.5' magic, so models from other minor versions are refused.

read_unchecked was removed in 0.5.2, so the published benchmark harness (which calls it) does not build against current releases as written. A fix for huge allocations from an untrusted matrix.def header (#167, 2026-10-03) is on master only, not in crates.io 0.5.2.

Harness flaws behind the numbers: the timed Vibrato loop only counts tokens while MeCab's -Owakati parse() builds an output string; only the Rust side was built with +avx2; MeCab mmaps its dictionary, so its timed loop likely absorbs page faults that Vibrato paid during the untimed load (inference); runs were not pinned to a core on the hybrid P/E-core i9-12900K. The non-compatible default mode matters little on this corpus: it has 47 ASCII spaces in 10 of 2,346 lines.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick Vibrato over Vaporetto (same organisation, 21 ms on the same corpus) when you need MeCab-dictionary lattice output with IPADIC or UniDic POS features rather than pointwise word boundaries from a KyTea-style model; jieba-rs is the analogue for Chinese, not Japanese.
verified_claims_summary: On the authors' tokenizer-speed-bench (tag vibrato-0.5.0-benchmark), tokenizing the 2,346 lines of 'I Am a Cat' on an i9-12900K took 42 ms with Vibrato 0.5.0 vs 87 ms with MeCab 2020-09-14 on IPADIC 2.7.0, and 75 vs 179 ms on unidic-cwj 3.1.1 (about 2.1x and 2.4x, derived from page data); MeCab was built -O3 by its own configure with GCC (version not stated), Vibrato with cargo --release plus +avx2, and dictionary loading was excluded from the timing.
status_note: Maintained (master commits through 2026-10-03, last crates.io release 0.5.2 in March 2025, MIT OR Apache-2.0); the benchmark is first-party, dates from v0.5.0 (February 2023), and issue #96 to refresh it is still open, while its harness gives MeCab extra output formatting and a non-AVX2 build and leaves dictionary load time (Vibrato's weak spot) out of the measurement.
